title: The Heavens Declare, the Law Revives
summary: The psalm begins with the silent speech of the sky, which proclaims God's glory day and night to the whole earth, and with the sun running its course like a bridegroom and a champion. It then turns to the law of the LORD, which is perfect, trustworthy, and sweeter than honey. It ends with a personal prayer for cleansing from hidden faults and willful sins, asking that the psalmist's words and thoughts be pleasing to God, his Rock and Redeemer.
story: Psalm 19 comes right after the great royal song of Psalm 18 and just before the royal prayers of Psalms 20 and 21. Several scholars have noticed that Psalms 15 to 24 seem arranged around it: two entrance psalms (15 and 24), two songs of trust (16 and 23), two laments (17 and 22), and royal psalms on either side (18, and 20 and 21), with Psalm 19 and its praise of God's law at the center. Whether or not the arrangement was intentional, the placement makes a point the Psalter keeps making from Psalm 1 onward: the king and the people live well only by God's instruction. The psalm gathers two great themes of the Bible's opening pages, creation and the law given at Sinai, and holds them together in one song.
historical:
The superscription reads For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. For the choirmaster translates a Hebrew term whose meaning is not certain; most take it to mean the director of the temple music, and it appears in fifty-five psalm headings. Tradition reads of David as authorship; many modern scholars see the headings as early editorial notes and think the psalm's two halves may once have been separate poems, a hymn about creation (verses 1 to 6) and a meditation on the law (verses 7 to 14), joined by an editor. Others argue that the psalm was composed as a unity, since the two halves are deliberately balanced and linked by the theme of speech and light.

The psalm names no event, and its date is uncertain. Its praise of the Torah as a delight rather than a burden has parallels in Psalms 1 and 119, which many date after the exile, while traditional readers place it in David's time. What is clear is that it belongs to a world in which Israel's neighbors worshiped the heavenly bodies, and it answers that world directly.
cultural:
Across the ancient Near East the sun was a god. In Mesopotamia the sun god Shamash was also the god of justice, who saw everything under heaven and upheld law; the famous law code of Hammurabi shows the king receiving authority from him. Psalm 19 sets the sun and the law side by side, but in a very different order. The sun is not a god. It lives in a tent God pitched for it, and it runs the course God set. Justice and wisdom come not from the sun but from the law of the LORD, which gives light to the eyes. Nothing escapes the sun's heat, the psalm says, but it is God's word that searches the heart.

The images of verse 5 come from ordinary life. A bridegroom came out from the wedding canopy or chamber radiant with joy, and a champion was a mighty warrior or runner eager to race. Gold and honey in verse 10 were the most precious and the sweetest things an ancient Israelite knew; wild honey, often found in rock crevices, was a rare delight.
literary: The psalm falls into three parts. Verses 1 to 6 are a creation hymn in which the heavens speak without speech; the paradox of verses 3 and 4 is deliberate, a voice with no sound that nevertheless reaches the ends of the world. Verses 7 to 9 are six tightly built lines, each naming the law by a different word (law, testimony, precepts, commandments, fear, judgments), each giving it a quality, and most giving an effect. In the first part God is called El, the general word for God; in the second the covenant name, the LORD, appears seven times. The movement is from the universal to the personal: from what all people can see in the sky, to what Israel heard at Sinai, to the psalmist's own heart. The final verse turns the psalm itself into an offering, asking that its words be pleasing to God.

outline.t: The perfect law of the LORD
More precious than gold, sweeter than honey
A prayer for cleansing: my Rock and my Redeemer

doctrines.note: The psalm holds together two ways God makes himself known: through what he has made, which speaks to every nation, and through his word, which revives the soul and makes the simple wise. Theologians call these general and special revelation. The first shows God's glory; the second shows his will and brings a person into covenant with him.
The law here is not a burden but a gift, perfect, right, radiant, and sweet. Torah means instruction, and the psalm treats it as the loving guidance of a covenant God.

Verses 12 and 13 distinguish hidden faults, which a person cannot even see in himself, from willful sins, which he knows and chooses. The psalmist asks God to deal with both, recognizing that self-knowledge is limited.

words.note: Torah, law or instruction. Its range runs from a parent's teaching (Proverbs 1:8) to the whole body of God's commands given through Moses. Here it is the first of six names for God's word, and its effect is reviving the soul, literally turning it back or restoring it. The psalm's joy in the law shows that Torah was experienced as life, not merely as rules.

Shemesh, sun. The Hebrew word is close kin to Shamash, the name of the Mesopotamian sun god. The psalm uses the ordinary word but denies it any divinity: the sun lives in a tent God pitched and runs a course God set. Its glory is borrowed.

Ga'al, to redeem, here as a title, my Redeemer. A redeemer (go'el) in Israel was the nearest relative, who bought back family land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or protected the family's name (Leviticus 25:25, Ruth 4). To call God my Redeemer is to call him the family member who takes responsibility for you.

Higgayon, meditation, the murmuring or musing of the heart. The related verb describes the low reading aloud of the one who meditates on God's law in Psalm 1:2. The psalmist asks that not only his spoken words but his inward thoughts be pleasing to God.

christ: Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans 10:18: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.” He applies the silent preaching of the heavens to the spread of the gospel message to Israel and the nations, a creative use that assumes God has always intended his word to reach everyone. In Romans 1:20 he makes a related argument, that God's power and divine nature have been clearly seen in what he has made. The New Testament also presents Jesus as the fullest word of God: John calls him the Word through whom all things were made and the true light who gives light to everyone (John 1:1-9). The psalm itself doesn't speak of the Messiah. The link is that the same God who speaks in creation and in the law speaks finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2), and that the Redeemer the psalmist prays to is the one the New Testament names in Christ.
questions: The heavens speak without words. When have you sensed something of God in the created world, and what did it say to you?
The psalmist calls God's law sweeter than honey. What would need to change for God's instruction to feel like a delight rather than a burden to you?
Verse 12 asks, “Who can discern his own errors?” Who in your life helps you see faults you can't see yourself?
